title: Why spelling misbehaves
text: English spelling is a museum of pronunciation. Each letter survived a reform that never came, and every irregularity is a fossil {{1}} something: the silent k in knife is the Old English pronunciation, kept visible; the gh of 'though' {{2}} a sound that disappeared from the language but not from the page. The Great Vowel Shift — the long, slow {{3}} of English vowels between 1400 and 1700 — happened almost entirely {{4}} spelling had begun to standardise, which is why we write the vowels of Chaucer and speak the vowels of Shakespeare. Printing poured concrete into the mess: early typesetters, often trained in Dutch, {{5}} extra letters wherever it suited their presses, and 'debt' gained its silent b purely to {{6}} scholars of its Latin origin, debitum. Reformers have {{7}} ever since — Webster pruned American spellings by decree, and George Bernard Shaw left money to design a new alphabet — but each attempt collides with the {{8}} of four centuries of printed habit. English spelling, in short, is not wrong; it is late. It records where the language was, not where it went.

gaps.explanation: 'a fossil recording something' — preserving the evidence of it; retain = keep for oneself.
'the gh commemorates a sound' — memorialises what is gone; commence = begin.
'the slow migration of English vowels' — their journey from one pronunciation to another; imitation = copying.
'happened once spelling had begun to standardise' — after it had started; 'even' and 'only' do not introduce a time clause.
'typesetters inserted extra letters' — placed them in; assert = state firmly.
'to remind scholars of its Latin origin' — 'remind somebody of something' is the fixed pattern; reclaim = recover.
'reformers have persisted ever since' — kept trying; desist = stop, the opposite; consist takes 'of'.
'collides with the inertia of four centuries of habit' — the drag of the status quo; incision = a surgical cut.
